claims.text: Doping an oxide support with selected foreign cations enhances the electronic interaction between the support and supported transition-metal nanoparticles.
Support doping increases charge transfer from the oxide support to the metal nanoparticles.
Increased charge transfer to metal nanoparticles changes the adsorption of reaction intermediates.
Charge-transfer-induced changes in intermediate adsorption can enhance catalytic activity.
The controlled comparison can keep nanoparticle size, dispersion, and morphology unchanged while changing only support doping.
Introducing dopant cations alters the intrinsic electronic structure of the oxide support.
A shift in the metal d-band center can serve as evidence of enhanced metal-support charge transfer.
Metal core-level XPS binding-energy shifts can indicate charge transfer to Pt or Pd.
XAS signatures can establish enhanced charge transfer at a doped-oxide/metal interface.
Support doping will cause a downward shift in the metal d-band center relative to an undoped-support baseline.
Catalysts on doped supports will have higher reaction rates or turnover frequencies than otherwise identical catalysts on undoped supports.
The hypothesis is restricted to reactions and conditions in which metal-support electronic interactions dominate catalytic behavior.
The hypothesis assumes that support doping does not inadvertently change nanoparticle geometry.
The magnitude of electronic and catalytic changes depends on dopant identity and concentration.
Support doping may introduce uncontrolled changes in nanoparticle morphology.
Simultaneous absence of an electronic-structure change and catalytic improvement relative to the undoped control would falsify the proposed pathway.
